questions.q: What is the primary goal of sharding a database?
options: Keeping a synchronized full copy of the data on every node
Reducing query latency by caching hot rows in memory
Encrypting different tables with different keys per tenant
Splitting data across nodes so no single machine stores or serves it all

questions.q: How does hash partitioning assign a row to a shard?
options: By the row's insertion timestamp, rotating through the shards on an hourly cycle
By hashing the shard key and mapping the digest into a shard slot
By the row's size, placing large rows on high-capacity shards
By the region of the client that first wrote the row

questions.q: What key advantage does range partitioning hold over hash partitioning?
options: Rows adjacent in key order stay together, making range scans efficient
It can never produce hot spots regardless of how skewed the access pattern becomes
It requires no metadata service to locate a key's shard
Rows are perfectly evenly distributed without tuning

questions.q: What is a 'hot spot' in a sharded system?
options: A shard whose disks run at higher temperature under sustained load
A key range that has been cached in memory by every shard
One shard receiving a disproportionate share of traffic or data
The coordinator node that routes every query in the cluster

questions.q: Why is the choice of shard key so consequential?
options: It permanently sets the database's on-disk page size across every shard
It determines data spread and which queries can stay on one shard
It fixes the number of shards permanently at creation time
It controls which replication mode each shard may use

questions.q: A query filters on a column that is not part of the shard key. What must the router typically do?
options: Reject the query, since non-key filters are unsupported
Route it to the first shard, which then proxies the request to the others in sequence
Answer it from the routing metadata without touching shards
Broadcast (scatter-gather) the query to all shards and merge results

questions.q: Time-ordered IDs as a range-sharding key create which classic problem?
options: Old shards keep growing forever as history accumulates on them
Range lookups by ID must always touch every single shard in the cluster
All new writes land on the newest shard, creating a write hot spot
IDs collide across shards because time is not unique

questions.q: Why do sharded systems often pre-create many more logical partitions than physical nodes?
options: Rebalancing becomes moving whole partitions, not re-splitting data
Each logical partition needs a dedicated physical disk to stay properly isolated
Query planners require partition counts to be powers of two
More partitions increase the replication factor automatically

questions.q: A multi-tenant app shards by tenant_id. One tenant grows to 30% of all traffic. What happens?
options: The router automatically and transparently splits that tenant's rows across several shards
That tenant's shard saturates while others idle, since a tenant cannot span shards here
Traffic rebalances naturally as the hash function redistributes keys
The tenant's queries slow down only for cross-tenant joins

questions.q: Why does naive modulo (key % N) sharding make adding a node painful?
options: Modulo arithmetic overflows once N exceeds the key's bit width
New nodes can only accept keys written after they joined
Changing N remaps most keys, forcing a massive data shuffle
The modulo must be recomputed per query, doubling read latency

questions.q: An order and its line items are always fetched together. What does sharding both by order_id give you?
options: A guarantee that orders are globally sorted by creation time
Cross-shard transactions become unnecessary for any query in the system
Line items compress better because they share a shard file
Related rows co-locate, so the common query stays single-shard

questions.q: What makes cross-shard joins expensive?
options: Rows must be shipped between nodes and joined outside their home shards
Every participating shard must first be locked to freeze its data for the join's duration
Join results must be written back to every participating shard
The SQL parser reparses the query once per participating shard

questions.q: During live resharding, how do systems avoid downtime while moving a partition?
options: They pause only the reads, because writes can always be replayed later from the log
They move data at night when traffic is assumed to be zero
They copy the partition while streaming ongoing changes, then cut over briefly
They drop the partition and rebuild it from a recent backup

questions.q: A unique username constraint must hold across all shards. Why is this harder than on one database?
options: Uniqueness now needs a global check or a dedicated service, not one local index
Unique indexes cannot exist on sharded tables at all
Hash collisions between shards create duplicate usernames
Each individual shard enforces its uniqueness constraint only for reads and never for writes

questions.q: Why do many systems route by a directory (lookup service) instead of pure hashing?
options: Directories eliminate the need for shard replicas entirely
Hashing cannot address more than 64 shards in practice
A directory service removes the query router as a single point of failure entirely
Explicit mappings allow targeted moves of hot keys without global remapping

questions.q: An analytics query must aggregate across all shards nightly. Reasonable pattern?
options: Run it against the primary shard, which keeps summary copies of the others by default
Scatter the query, pre-aggregate per shard, and merge the partial results
Temporarily merge all shards onto one node for the query window
Disable writes cluster-wide so the aggregate is consistent

questions.q: A celebrity user makes a single key hot beyond one shard's capacity. Which mitigation works?
options: Salt the key into sub-keys spread across shards, merging on read
Raise that shard's replication factor so followers absorb the writes
Move the key to the coordinator node, which has spare capacity
Enable synchronous replication so the writes are shared evenly

questions.q: Two-phase commit coordinates a cross-shard transaction. What is its well-known failure mode?
options: Committed data is written twice, doubling storage on both shards
The prepare phase deadlocks unless shards share a physical clock
Participants auto-abort after prepare, so commits rarely succeed
A crashed coordinator can leave participants blocked, holding locks in doubt

questions.q: Geo-sharding places EU users' data in EU shards for latency and residency. What new problem appears?
options: EU shards must run an entirely different database engine to comply with residency law
Interactions between users in different regions require slow cross-region queries
Hash functions behave differently across regions, corrupting routing
Latency inside the EU rises because the shards are smaller

questions.q: Your shard map lives in ZooKeeper; routers cache it. A partition moves and a router's cache is stale. Robust handling?
options: Routers drop all traffic until an operator manually reloads every cache
Shards accept any key and forward misroutes in a nightly batch job
The old shard rejects misrouted requests with a hint, and the router refreshes its map
TTL the cache at one week to keep the ZooKeeper load minimal
